channel_name: This Week in Startups · Jason Calacanis
video_title: VC experts on why Physical AI funding is heating up | E2333
gist: In a This Week in Startups VC roundtable, Jason Calacanis hosts Paige (Behind Genius Ventures) and Caitlin Holloway (776) to unpack a physical-AI funding boom (~$50B in H1 2026, up 80% YoY), the Pentagon's new ChatGPT/Grok deployment (Claude notably excluded), 776's 15x-marked-up StarCloud orbital-data-center bet, EU AI regulation, and a growing venture consensus that frontier AI labs will eventually compete with the vertical-app customers they serve.

insights.claim: Physical AI companies raised almost $50 billion in venture funding in the first half of 2026 alone, up 80% from all of 2025, meaning six months of 2026 outraised 2022, 2023, and 2024 combined.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: A step-change acceleration in capital formation for hardware/robotics/defense-adjacent AI signals the category has moved from niche to mainstream institutional allocation; watch for valuation compression risk if the pace can't be sustained.
insights.quote: Physical AI companies now have raised almost 50 billion in venture funding, wait for it, in the first half of 2026, up 80% from 2025.

insights.claim: Deal volume in physical AI hit roughly 450 deals and $45 billion in the first half of 2026, compared with fewer than five deals in 2023 by the same measure shown on-screen.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: The near-vertical deal-count curve is itself a bubble-vs-secular-shift tell that investors should track quarter over quarter for signs of a plateau or blow-off top.
insights.quote: 450 deals and 45 billion in physical AI in the first half 26 back in 23 it was not even five.

insights.claim: Aerospace and defense are currently the top two spending categories within the physical AI funding surge.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Capital is concentrating in the sub-verticals with the clearest government/defense demand pull, which is a narrower and more policy-sensitive bet than 'physical AI' broadly implies.

insights.claim: 776's Caitlin Holloway uses shifts in where the best engineering talent wants to work as a leading indicator for sector conviction: a decade ago the smartest engineers she met wanted to work on ads (ad tech); today the equivalent engineer wants to build rocket engines in Moses Lake, Washington, because the work feels connected to a meaningful mission.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Holloway (776)
insights.so_what: Talent migration toward hardware/deep-tech missions is a non-obvious, hard-to-fake signal investors can track (e.g. via hiring data, LinkedIn moves) as a leading indicator ahead of capital flows.
insights.quote: 10 years ago, the smartest engineer I met, they they wanted to work on ads. today. That engineer, she wants to build rocket engines in Moses Lake, Washington.

insights.claim: 776 treats Jensen Huang's prediction that 'every industrial company will become a robotics company' as directionally prophetic rather than self-serving Nvidia marketing, and it shapes how the firm evaluates whether the physical-AI boom is a bubble.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Holloway (776)
insights.so_what: If a major LP-facing VC is underwriting deals partly on this framing, it suggests robotics-enablement plays across legacy industrial companies (not just pure-play robotics startups) could be a durable multi-year theme.
insights.quote: Jensen very famously predicted that every industrial company will become a robotics company.

themes.theme: Pentagon AI Rollout and Autonomous Weapons

insights.claim: The Pentagon (Department of War) completed an eight-month rollout of custom versions of ChatGPT and Grok for its roughly 3 million military personnel, adding to an existing Gemini deployment; Anthropic's Claude is notably absent from the platform following an earlier dispute with the department over usage restrictions.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Being excluded from the largest single government AI buyer is a real commercial cost for Anthropic and reflects its more restrictive stance on military use cases versus OpenAI and xAI — a differentiator investors in AI labs should price in.
insights.quote: Claude is missing entirely uh from the platform.

insights.claim: Per the Pentagon rollout terms, neither OpenAI nor xAI trains its models on Department of War data.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: This data-isolation guarantee is likely a template other sensitive enterprise/government buyers will demand from frontier labs going forward.
insights.quote: Neither vendor trains models on Pentagon or DOW Department of War data.

insights.claim: The two military AI products are functionally specialized: ChatGPT Gov/ML handles paperwork, logistics and policy work, while Grok for Government (delivered via SpaceX's Starshield) handles supply-chain analysis, faster ops analysis, and adaptive-reasoning 'playbooks' — implying a split rather than single-vendor government AI market.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Government AI procurement is fragmenting by use case rather than consolidating around one vendor, which supports a multi-winner rather than winner-take-all investment thesis in gov-AI.

insights.claim: Selling AI/software into the government used to be considered an early-stage venture death trap because of multi-year sales cycles; Caitlin Holloway says the real bottleneck has now flipped — winning the contract is easier, but a 30-person startup must deliver against obligations that used to require a 100+ person vendor, and that delivery risk is the new challenge.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Holloway (776)
insights.so_what: Diligence on gov-tech/defense startups should shift from 'can they win the contract' to 'can they operationally deliver and retain the contract,' which is a different (and less obvious) failure mode to underwrite.
insights.quote: I think the bottleneck used to be winning the contract, but now it's really just surviving one.

insights.claim: Government and defense contracts often arrive as non-dilutive capital or revenue in amounts that catch founders by surprise, forcing them to quickly figure out whether that revenue is durable and whether the contracts will be renewed.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Holloway (776)
insights.so_what: Investors should stress-test defense-tech revenue quality (renewal risk, program dependency) separately from typical SaaS retention metrics.

insights.claim: Jason relays that Boston Dynamics' interim CEO told him at a Paris robotics conference that China is almost certainly weaponizing robots (e.g., mounting guns on quadruped 'dog-style' robots) and that no Chinese-made robotics should be allowed into the US for national-security reasons — from which Jason infers the US should assume adversaries are pursuing autonomous soldiers.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: A direct industry-insider claim that a geopolitical rival is actively weaponizing legged robots supports higher conviction in US autonomous-ground-robotics and counter-robotics defense spending as a durable theme.

insights.claim: The UN is developing a treaty framework called LAWS (Lethal Autonomous Weapon Systems) aimed at governing autonomous weapons.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Emerging international regulatory frameworks around autonomous weapons could become a compliance and export-control variable for defense-robotics investors to monitor, similar to arms-control regimes.

insights.claim: Jason predicts that future warfare will shift away from drone-only engagements toward scenarios where autonomous ground robots (e.g., 'a hundred robots' landing on a beach) secure territory, a qualitatively different mode of conflict than current fixed-wing or quadcopter drone warfare.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: If autonomous ground combat robotics becomes a real near-term military requirement, it opens a new investable defense-robotics sub-category distinct from today's drone-focused defense tech portfolio.

themes.theme: StarCloud: The Orbital Data Center Bet

insights.claim: Orbital-data-center startup StarCloud raised $250 million at a $2.3 billion valuation, led by Manhattan West, with Nvidia and Cisco participating as investors — a raise that more than doubled the company's valuation from five months earlier.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Strategic participation from Nvidia and Cisco (not just financial VCs) signals the incumbents view orbital compute as a credible extension of their core businesses, not a novelty bet.

insights.claim: StarCloud put the first H100 GPU chip into orbit in 2025, and Nvidia is now using StarCloud's in-flight telemetry data to design its first chip built specifically for space deployment.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: A startup's flight data directly shaping a chip giant's product roadmap is a strong signal of technical credibility and durable strategic-partner lock-in, reducing single-customer risk for StarCloud.

insights.claim: 776 led StarCloud's seed round roughly two years ago at approximately a $150 million valuation after Caitlin Holloway met founder Philip by chance seated next to him at a dinner (not a formal pitch) at Founders Forum in the Cotswolds; the new $2.3 billion valuation represents roughly a 15x markup, and 776 views the position as a likely fund-returner.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Holloway (776)
insights.so_what: A single seed check turning into a probable fund-returner within two years illustrates how concentrated the return profile of the current physical-AI/space-tech cycle can be for early movers with founder-access edge.
insights.quote: So, so we got in at um a buck 50. Um and so it's now at 2.3.

insights.claim: StarCloud has multiple SpaceX launches booked for 2027 to continue deploying its orbital data-center satellites.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: StarCloud's roadmap execution remains dependent on SpaceX launch cadence, tying its near-term growth trajectory to a supplier that is also viewed as a long-term competitor in orbital infrastructure.

insights.claim: The cost to launch one kilogram into orbit fell from roughly $10,000 in 2014 to about $4,000 in 2026 (driven largely by SpaceX), with projections of roughly $1,500 by 2030 and as low as $273 by 2040 — this cost curve was a key quantitative input to 776's decision to back StarCloud.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: A continuing multi-decade decline in launch cost is the structural tailwind underwriting the entire orbital-infrastructure investment category (data centers, manufacturing, solar) — a useful macro variable to track for the whole space-tech sector.

insights.claim: 776's 'infrastructure for the inevitable' framework: if you believe a macro trend (e.g., falling launch costs, AI's rise) is inevitable, invest upstream in suppliers that labs, primes, or incumbents will become structurally reliant on — both for revenue and for proprietary learning/data access — rather than building 'downstream of a lab.' The firm applies this same logic to HGEN, an on-site hydrogen production company for heavy industry in Southern California positioned to displace natural gas.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Holloway (776)
insights.so_what: A repeatable, transferable investment heuristic — back suppliers of inevitable trends rather than application-layer plays dependent on incumbents — that other investors could apply across AI, space, and industrial re-shoring themes.

themes.theme: SpaceX as the Space Economy's Single Point of Failure

insights.claim: Caitlin Holloway states that essentially the entire American space launch economy currently runs on one company's (SpaceX) launch manifest, calling it a single point of failure shared not just by StarCloud but by Stoke Space and even the Pentagon.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Holloway (776)
insights.so_what: Any disruption to SpaceX's launch cadence (regulatory, technical, or geopolitical) would be a systemic risk across the entire US space-tech portfolio, not an isolated company risk — worth explicit scenario planning for space-tech LPs.

insights.claim: 776 portfolio company Stoke Space is building what Caitlin Holloway describes as the first rocket where both stages successfully return and refly, and she frames the goal as building a second 'airline' for space (Stoke's Nova as the 'delivery van' versus SpaceX Starship as the 'cargo ship') rather than a head-to-head Starship competitor.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Holloway (776)
insights.so_what: Positioning a launch startup as complementary capacity (a different payload class/use case) rather than a direct SpaceX competitor is a differentiated way to underwrite launch-sector risk.

insights.claim: Despite the competitive narrative between StarCloud and SpaceX's own Starlink/space-data ambitions, the two companies collaborate closely in practice — StarCloud's satellite laser communication units (nicknamed 'Cheddar') were hand-delivered by SpaceX ahead of launch.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Holloway (776)
insights.so_what: Operational camaraderie between nominal 'competitors' in space-tech suggests the sector functions more like a shared-infrastructure ecosystem than a zero-sum market, which should temper concerns about SpaceX crowding out orbital-compute startups.

themes.theme: EU AI Regulation and the Contrarian Europe Trade

insights.claim: The EU formally designated ChatGPT a 'Very Large Online Search Engine' under the Digital Services Act, subjecting OpenAI to the same obligations as Google and Bing: annual audits, published risk assessments, and regulator access to data, with fines of up to 6% of global revenue for non-compliance — a figure that would run into billions of dollars for a company OpenAI's or Anthropic's size.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: A 6%-of-global-revenue penalty regime is a material tail risk for large AI platforms operating in the EU and could shape where frontier labs choose to headquarter, launch, or restrict certain product features.

insights.claim: Reddit and Roblox have also been swept into related EU regulatory designations alongside ChatGPT under the same push.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: The EU's platform-regulation net is widening beyond pure search/AI companies to consumer social and gaming platforms, broadening compliance-cost exposure across the tech sector.

insights.claim: Caitlin Holloway argues the ChatGPT search-engine designation has near-zero near-term impact on seed-stage startups (a 15-person company won't be designated), but expects the definitions to eventually surface as compliance questionnaires within enterprise sales cycles a few years out.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Holloway (776)
insights.so_what: Early-stage investors should monitor EU AI regulation as a slow-moving enterprise-sales/compliance headwind rather than an immediate portfolio risk, and time diligence questions accordingly.

insights.claim: Caitlin Holloway takes a contrarian view that US VCs' widespread mockery of European regulation (often voiced while vacationing in Tuscany or the South of France) obscures real opportunity — she specifically flags Zurich, Switzerland as producing world-class physics and quantum computing talent that is dramatically undercapitalized because of anti-Europe narrative bias, saying she'd rather back a strong Zurich quant team at a fair price than another 'agent wrapper' startup.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Holloway (776)
insights.so_what: A specific, named geographic and technical thesis (Zurich quantum/physics talent) that an investor could act on directly by sourcing deals in that market rather than defaulting to the anti-Europe consensus.
insights.quote: if I if I had $100, I would much rather back a brilliant quant team in Zurich.

insights.claim: Paige describes portfolio company Mezzo deliberately building its AI compliance engine first for the EU's heavily regulated environment ('eat the frog') on the theory that succeeding under the hardest regulatory regime first makes later expansion into less-regulated markets comparatively easy.
insights.speaker: Paige (Behind Genius Ventures)
insights.so_what: Heavy regulation can function as a competitive moat rather than purely a cost center for well-capitalized startups willing to build compliance-first, favoring incumbents who can absorb the upfront legal/compliance spend.

insights.claim: Entrepreneur First's newly opened San Francisco hub is cited as a strong pipeline bringing highly capable European founders to build companies in the US.
insights.speaker: Paige (Behind Genius Ventures)
insights.so_what: A concrete, named sourcing channel for European founder talent relocating to the US that investors could track for deal flow.

themes.theme: Frontier Lab Distrust and Vertical AI Defensibility

insights.claim: Anthropic reversed its data-retention policy after major enterprise pushback tied to fears that it was training itself to become 'the last company' (a description Dario Amodei denies Anthropic used internally), moving to a 30-day retention window with data held in the customer's own cloud environment rather than Anthropic's servers.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: A frontier lab reversing policy under enterprise pressure is itself evidence that large AI buyers now have real negotiating leverage over lab data practices — a shift Caitlin Holloway says would have been unthinkable 18 months ago.

insights.claim: There is a widely held belief in the venture and startup community (stated as consensus, not confirmed fact) that frontier labs will eventually use customer usage data and reinforcement-learning signal to build competing vertical products — citing Anthropic's Claude Code as having competed with Cursor and Claude for design as competing with Figma as precedent, with similar dynamics feared in legal and biotech verticals.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Startups building thin wrappers on top of a single frontier model face a structural existential risk that should factor into valuation and moat analysis for any vertical-AI-application investment.

insights.claim: Jason draws a direct parallel between the current frontier-lab dynamic and Fred Wilson's (Union Square Ventures) 'be your own platform' thesis from the social-media API era, when Facebook and Twitter studied which third-party API use cases were growing fastest and then absorbed those features natively — arguing today's version is higher-stakes because it involves proprietary intelligence and trade secrets, not just a feature or social graph.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: A historical analogy investors can use to underwrite platform-dependency risk in AI application startups: watch which product categories a frontier lab's own usage data shows heavy demand for, since those are the most likely to be absorbed.

insights.claim: In response to platform-dependency risk, some vertical AI companies are building their own smaller, in-house or on-prem language models: legal AI company referred to as 'Lora' (likely Harvey) reportedly built small vertical language models so individual law firms (named: Sherman & Sterling, Wilson Sonsini, Orrick) can run on-prem or on their own cloud; separately, 'GoAI' (rebranded from Abacus/Aboc, sourced through the 776/Behind Genius Ventures accelerator) offers a plug-in on-prem AI appliance that reportedly deploys in about 15 minutes and recently raised at a strong valuation.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: On-prem/vertical small-language-model infrastructure is emerging as a concrete, fundable response to frontier-lab dependency risk — a specific sub-category (enterprise on-prem LLM appliances) to watch for further deal flow.

insights.claim: Jason predicts that thin-wrapper AI companies (naming ElevenLabs and Lovable) that pass large volumes of frontier-lab tokens through to end users are structurally exposed, because once frontier labs come under investor pressure to monetize, any implicit courtesy of not competing with major customers will disappear.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Investors in wrapper-style AI companies should specifically underwrite the scenario where the underlying model provider launches a competing first-party product once profit pressure mounts.
insights.quote: When you get taken to the woodshed and your stocks like on the floor, which could happen, you know, if they if they don't have profits.

themes.theme: VC Fund Mechanics and Thesis-Generation Playbooks

insights.claim: Both guest VCs flag that physical-AI startups now often raise extremely large rounds very quickly, creating real ownership-dilution risk for small early checks even amid a hot fundraising market.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Sizing pre-seed/seed checks in capital-intensive physical AI requires modeling aggressive follow-on dilution scenarios, not just headline valuation growth.

insights.claim: Behind Genius Ventures mitigates physical-AI dilution risk by focusing on verticalized applications of physical AI (rather than general-purpose physical AI platforms), which the firm says reach revenue and commercialization faster and show less severe dilution dynamics.
insights.speaker: Paige (Behind Genius Ventures)
insights.so_what: A specific, testable sub-sector allocation rule (vertical over general-purpose) for navigating a capital-intensive category with high dilution risk.

insights.claim: Behind Genius Ventures writes roughly 25 to 30 similarly sized checks per fund vintage at pre-seed and seed and very rarely doubles down; when it does increase ownership, it is typically in a pre-seed-to-seed continuation, while the firm still has an asymmetric information advantage and before valuation gets extreme.
insights.speaker: Paige (Behind Genius Ventures)
insights.so_what: A concrete portfolio-construction template (broad initial bets, disciplined and rare follow-on) that illustrates one specific way early-stage funds manage power-law outcomes without concentrated follow-on risk.

insights.claim: Behind Genius Ventures has driven roughly $10 million of additional LP capital directly onto its portfolio companies' cap tables via co-investment/pro-rata sourcing for its LP base, largely without taking carry on that capital — a practice both Jason and Caitlin Holloway suggest the firm should reconsider and start monetizing via an SPV structure.
insights.speaker: Paige (Behind Genius Ventures)
insights.so_what: An emerging fund is currently leaving a monetizable revenue stream (carry on sourced co-investment capital) on the table, which is a fixable economics gap as the firm matures.

insights.claim: Both funds describe VC secondaries as having gone from a taboo, 'swept under the rug' topic to now generating the majority of exits/distributions industry-wide, driven by IPOs being pushed out to year 12-20 or never happening at all (Stripe cited as an example), prompting both firms to proactively discuss liquidity planning with their LP advisory committees.
insights.speaker: Paige (Behind Genius Ventures)
insights.so_what: Secondary-market liquidity has become the primary distribution mechanism for venture funds, not an exception — LPs and fund managers should plan around secondaries as core strategy rather than a fallback.

insights.claim: 776 discloses to founders upfront, as an early-stage/accelerator-style fund, that it has a fiduciary obligation to trim its pro-rata position pari passu with other sellers as a company crosses roughly $500 million, $1 billion, and $2 billion valuation marks — a fund-level discipline contrasted with Jason's personal angel practice of never selling shares in Robinhood, Uber, Nubank, or DoorDash held since their seed rounds, since fund maturity (needing DPI by fund IV) forces distribution in a way personal capital does not.
insights.speaker: Caitlin Holloway (776)
insights.so_what: Founders and co-investors should expect institutional seed funds to sell down winners at defined valuation milestones regardless of continued conviction, which affects cap-table dynamics and secondary supply timing around breakout companies.

insights.claim: Paige's applied/multimodal-AI investment thesis originated from a 2024 conference conversation with an LP who had helped build Qualcomm's wearables business; the thesis directly led to Behind Genius Ventures' $500,000 investment — the firm's largest check at the time — in Manva, an edge-AI factory-floor quality and safety company, whose founder was won over specifically after reading Paige's published thesis writing; Manva later raised a Series A from USVP in under a year.
insights.speaker: Paige (Behind Genius Ventures)
insights.so_what: A concrete example of published investment-thesis writing directly generating superior deal access (the founder chose Paige because of her writing) and converting into a fast, credible follow-on round.

insights.claim: Jason's 'unmetered tokens' thesis: after being given unmetered access to a Bittensor-subnet API running Z.AI's GLM-4.5 model, he set it to run an autonomous, self-critiquing research loop every hour (later rewriting its own skill daily to improve) with no human oversight, concluding that once cheap-enough local compute (a roughly $10,000-$20,000 desktop) makes usage effectively unmetered, users effectively get 'a free human that doesn't sleep' — an argument for surging demand in local/edge AI hardware.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: If unmetered local inference becomes economically accessible, it reframes AI agent economics from a per-token cost model to a fixed-hardware-cost model, which could reshape demand for both consumer AI hardware and open-source model deployment tooling.
insights.quote: When you have unmetered, then this becomes like a free human. Like I'm I'm getting a free human that doesn't sleep that I can put on a task until I tell them to stop doing the task.

insights.claim: Jason predicts Apple's new CEO will move to acquire Perplexity, specifically citing its 'Perplexity Computer' product — a harness that runs an open-source model locally on Apple silicon first, falls back to a cheap model via OpenRouter, and only escalates to a frontier model as a last resort — as a route for Apple to build its own local-first AI search stack across iPhones, Mac Studios, and MacBooks with 128GB of RAM.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: A speculative but specific M&A thesis (Apple + Perplexity for on-device AI routing) that investors in either company, or in the on-device AI inference stack broadly, should watch for signs of validation.
